sociology_baseline.description: Owners are more persuadable by arguments that stay near existing views on affordability and repair necessity.
Visible support from a few respected owners could trigger broader meeting participation or opposition.
Renters are likely to withhold public views due to limited formal voice and dependence on owners.
Longtime residents, newer owners, and renters tend to discuss issues within similar-status networks.
Support for higher dues likely needs reinforcement from both technical evidence and neighbor endorsement.
Tenure and ownership status shape how fairness and responsibility are interpreted.
Attention may soften if boiler problems remain abstract, but rises quickly with any service disruption.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: Shared heating reliability makes infrastructure risk broadly legible across factions.
Monthly dues framing activates household budget concerns more than one-time abstract capital planning.
Transparent bids, reserve data, and fair meeting process can alter coalition formation.
Renters experience consequences without equivalent voting power, shaping informal pressure channels.
Longtime residents may anchor on prior board decisions or earlier maintenance episodes when evaluating credibility.
